local_attempts.prompt: Compare animal and plant cytokinesis and explain how their structures affect the mechanism.
local_attempts.first_response: Animal cytokinesis uses a contractile ring to pull the flexible membrane inward, making a deepening cleavage furrow. In a plant cell, the rigid wall remains in place while vesicles fuse between the nuclei and form a cell plate that grows outward; membranes and new wall material partition the daughters. Both mechanisms separate cytoplasm and do not copy DNA.
local_attempts.visible_evidence: L05 teaching-01: vesicles fuse between daughter nuclei; the plate grows outward; a rigid wall cannot pinch like an animal membrane. Actual plant pixels show two dark groups and a faint central partition.

local_attempts.prompt: Explain why an experiment showing more cells does not by itself prove successful tissue repair.
local_attempts.first_response: An increased cell count demonstrates proliferation, but repair also requires the right specialized cells arranged and connected to perform the lost function. For sensory tissue, useful signal transmission and appropriate connections, plus controlled growth, would support restoration. Extra cells alone could be disorganized or poorly functioning.
local_attempts.visible_evidence: L05 teaching-02: more cells alone do not establish the correct cell types, organization, connections, function and controlled growth.

local_attempts.prompt: Is meiosis I just mitosis performed on a diploid cell?

local_attempts.prompt: Explain how meiosis I reduces chromosome number without separating sister chromatids.
local_attempts.first_response: Each replicated homologue pairs with its corresponding partner in prophase I; the pairs line up in metaphase I. Anaphase I sends the two homologues to opposite poles while sister chromatids remain joined. Each daughter therefore receives one chromosome of each type, one complete set instead of two. Replicated copies remain, but the number of sets and chromosomes per daughter is halved.
local_attempts.visible_evidence: L06 teaching-01/02/03: homologues pair in prophase I, align as tetrads in metaphase I, and separate in anaphase I while sisters remain together, reducing two sets to one.

local_attempts.prompt: For a 2n = 8 species, describe chromosome and chromatid counts after meiosis I.
local_attempts.first_response: A 2n = 8 cell starts meiosis I with 8 chromosomes and 16 chromatids after replication. Each normal daughter after meiosis I has n = 4 chromosomes and 8 chromatids, one homologue of each type with two joined sister chromatids. Across both daughters the total remains 8 chromosomes and 16 chromatids.
local_attempts.visible_evidence: L06 teaching-03: one homologue of every type is one haploid set after meiosis I, despite chromosomes remaining replicated.

figure_observations.observation: Top animal cell narrows centrally; arrows point to two separate daughter-cell drawings. The lower edge of both daughter drawings is cropped flat; the complete outer outlines are not visible. Ring mechanism and genetic equality require text/model interpretation, not a photo of molecular events.

Two dark chromosome groups lie left and right of a faint vertical central partition; the rigid outer wall does not constrict centrally. Vesicles and outward growth are taught mechanisms, not directly resolved in this still micrograph.

Pale upper/right semicircle is meiosis I. Metaphase I has blue short above yellow short at left and green long above red long at right; poles are top and bottom. Anaphase I moves blue+green up and yellow+red down with exchanged tips and joined sister pairs. Figure is consistent with 2n=4; colors do not establish a whole-genome parental color key.
